newsitem.title: USA: High dollar may bite unsuspecting US corporations.
newsitem.headline: High dollar may bite unsuspecting US corporations.

text.p: Wall Street is more concerned than Corporate America that the rising dollar could take a bite out of 1997 profits, despite defensive actions taken by many businesses.
"We think the dollar is going to go higher and we think it is going to hurt corporate profits," said Dean Witter chief investment strategist Peter Canelo.

Canelo trimmed his forecast of 1997 earnings growth for the companies in the Standard & Poor's 500 index to 9 percent from 11 percent because of the dollar's strength, which means U.S. companies' sales overseas are worth less back at home.
The high-tech sector is the most vulnerable to the dollar's strength, according to J.P. Morgan global currency strategist Ron Levin.
In a report, J.P. Morgan said computer services companies, software firms, telecommunications equipment makers and semiconductor companies had the most to lose from a higher dollar.

Three brokerage firms Wednesday said they expect International Business Machines Corp.'s 1997 earnings to be hurt by the rise in the dollar, and IBM was left out in the cold during the market's rally.

The Dow Jones industrial average jumped 103.52 points to a record 6,961.63 and other market gauges also hit new highs, while IBM fell 25 cents to $145 in consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange.

Since Dec. 31, the dollar has risen 9.5 percent against the German mark and 7.2 percent vs. the Japanese yen. Despite a weekend meeting of the Group of Seven industrial nations at which officials said the dollar had risen enough, the currency has continued climbing.

Other companies with big international presences that could be hard hit are automakers such as Ford Motor Co. and General Motors Corp., General Electric Co., Philip Morris Cos., Coca-Cola Co. and big drug companies.
"I don't think the rising dollar has been priced into the drug stocks," said Salomon Brothers drug analyst Robert Uhl.

Despite the concerns, drug stocks jumped Wednesday and the American Stock Exchange Pharmaceutical Index rose nearly 2 percent to a record. Drug companies make a large percentage of their sales overseas.

"There is vulnerability for companies with cost bases principally in the United States," J.P. Morgan's Levin said. He said some industries, notably automakers, have shielded themselves from a higher dollar by going abroad to make many of the components used in U.S.-made cars.
Multinationals could get a "double whammy," said Tom Carpenter, chief economist for ASB Capital Management Inc., if their overseas results are also hit by stagnating economies in Japan and Europe.
"Most of the companies are confident that they are hedged out at least until year-end and possibly further, so it's not something to worry about near-term," said Salomon's Uhl.
"But at some point, it does unwind if the (dollar's) rise keeps going for an extended period of time," he said.
"Hedging" is a financial tool used to safeguard against volatile price movements. It works by fixing prices and margins in advance and cutting potential for losses.
